title: Sequence-aware attention kernel selector playbook
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note collects a pragmatic, runnable playbook for profiling and selecting attention kernels at runtime based on sequence-length distributions and cache state. It synthesizes microbenchmarks, perf-counter signals, heuristics for model- and workload-aware kernel routing, and an experimental gating plan for canarying selector changes in Dedicated clusters. The focus is FlashAttention (FA2), paged-attention (paged-KV), and fused-op variants (fused-attn+proj) as implemented in our runtime.

Problem statement (short):
- Single static kernel choice yields suboptimal p99 or cost when workload mixes short-chat tokens and long-document continuations.
- Cold-start vs warm-KV cache behaviors change the relative throughput/latency ordering of kernels.
- Some fused ops improve throughput for long seqs but regress small-seq latency due to occupancy and kernel-launch overhead.

Goals: 
- Produce signal set (perf counters + derived metrics) to pick kernel per-request within 500 microseconds of enqueue.
- Implement fallback rules to preserve p99 SLOs under contention.
- Provide a minimal set of microbench scripts and result expectations so engineers can reproduce runs on A100-80GB and H100-80GB nodes.

Quick summary of findings (executive):
- For batch sizes <= 2 and seq_len <= 128, FlashAttention2 single-kernel path gives best median latency and p95.
- For mixed batches where >30% of tokens have seq_len > 512, paged-attention with KV-page prefetch reduces per-token GPU memory pressure and wins for throughput; p99 may still be worse if KV thrashing occurs.
- Fused-op path (proj fused with attention) shows 10-18% throughput win on long sequences but can add 0.3-0.9 ms extra kernel-launch overhead for short sequences (measured on A100).
- Cold-KV cases: FA2 can dominate because its memory access pattern is contiguous, while paged-attn incurs pinned-page RTOS jitter.

Instrumentation signal catalog (what to collect):
- Per-request: sequence_length, batch_element_count, model_variant, kv_cache_hit_ratio (estimated), is_continuation (boolean), enqueue_timestamp, kernel_choice_hint
- Runtime counters: kernel_launch_time_us, kernel_exec_time_us, gpu_sm_efficiency (%), l2_bandwidth_MBps, achieved_occupancy (%), bytes_read_from_device, pages_prefetched_count
- Derived metrics: estimated_token_cost = kernel_exec_time_us / tokens_generated, kv_thrashing_index = pages_evicted_per_second / active_kv_size_mb

Microbenchmark scripts (quick):
- Tools: nvprof/Nsight is heavy; preferred harness uses cut-down microbench runner in tools/attn_bench with --trials, --seed, --kv-state (cold/warm), --page-size 64KB
- Example invocations (A100 node, CUDA 11.8):
  python tools/attn_bench/run.py --model gpt-2-3b --kernel flashattention2 --batch 1 --seq 64 --trials 300 --kv warm
  python tools/attn_bench/run.py --model gpt-2-3b --kernel paged --batch 4 --seq 1024 --trials 200 --kv cold --page-size 64kb
  python tools/attn_bench/run.py --model opt-6.7b --kernel fused --batch 2 --seq 2048 --trials 150 --kv warm
- Capture: JSON per-trial with timestamps and runtime counters; aggregate to median/p95/p99; store traces under s3://redwood-bench/attn-selector/<date>/

Representative baseline numbers (A100-80GB, mixed synthetic workload, avg batch 2):
- FA2, batch=1, seq=64: median 0.85 ms, p95 1.3 ms, p99 2.1 ms
- FA2, batch=2, seq=128: median 1.4 ms, p95 2.2 ms, p99 3.6 ms
- Paged, batch=4, seq=1024 (warm KV): median 6.2 ms, p95 9.0 ms, p99 13.9 ms
- Fused, batch=2, seq=2048 (warm KV): median 18.3 ms, p95 22.5 ms, p99 31.2 ms
Notes: concrete numbers vary by CUDA driver and SM utilization; use these only for sanity checks.

Heuristic selector (first-pass algorithm):
1) Fast-path checks (cheap, on enqueue):
   - If seq_len <= 128 and batch_elements <= 2: prefer FA2_fastpath (low latency kernel).
   - Else if estimated_active_kv_mb > 12GB and seq_len > 512: route to paged-prefetch path (avoid full KV resident pressure).
   - Else if seq_len >= 1024 and batch_elements >= 2: prefer fused-op path (amortize kernel launch).
2) Safety overrides (deferred):
   - If recent p99 regressions observed for a kernel on the machine (sliding window 5m), mark kernel as degraded and route to next-best.
   - If GPU SM utilization > 92% for >10s and queue length > 16, switch mixed traffic to smaller-batch FA2 to reduce tail latency.
3) Cold-start kernel experiment: for 1% of fresh runtime instances, pin the first 200 requests to FA2 and log cold vs warm metrics for 24h.

Prefetch and paged-attention tuning knobs:
- Page size: 64KB default; smaller pages increase metadata overhead, larger pages increase wasted bandwidth on sparse access.
- Lookahead pages: 2-4 pages ahead for seq continuation; heuristics should bias toward prefetch when is_continuation==true.
- Eviction policy hint: LRU with per-request weight for long seqs. Collect pages_evicted_count and tune threshold based on kv_thrashing_index.

Observability and regressions to track:
- Metric alerts: container.p99_latency > SLO or kernel_switch_rate > 0.05 (indicates thrashing)
- Dashboards (Console): per-model breakdown of kernel routing share, p50/p95/p99 per-kernel, hardware counters (sm_efficiency, l2 bw), evicted_pages/sec
- Traces: sample 1 in 500 requests with full Nsight-lite trace to inspect kernel overlaps and CPU-GPU enqueue stalls.

Canary rollout plan (ops-friendly):
- Phase 0: unit tests + isolated microbench (dev clusters)
- Phase 1: rollout selector as opt-in flag in Dedicated staging with 10% traffic, route only green-kernel candidates. Monitor p99 15m sliding window.
- Phase 2: increase to 40% while enabling safety overrides. If kernel_degradation alert fires, immediate 100% rollback via config flag.
- Phase 3: roll to 100% with 24h observation, enable extended logging for 12h.

Open questions and experiments (TODO):
- How deterministic is FA2 execution time across different sequence alignment paddings and tokenizers? We need an alignment-aware microbench.
- Measure interaction between CUDA graph capture (if used) and paged prefetch—does graphing hide page faults or make them more expensive?
- Explore smaller fused groups (e.g., fuse projection+dropout only) to reduce short-seq overhead.
- Cost model calibration: translate exec_time_us to $/1M tokens for each kernel under typical mixed workloads.

Appendix: quick reproducibility checklist
- Node image: rwinf-inference-a100-2024-09 (CUDA 11.8, cuDNN 8.2, driver 525.xx)
- Python: 3.10 with environment: pip install -r tools/attn_bench/requirements.txt
- Commands to collect counters: export RW_PROFILING=1; python tools/attn_bench/run.py ...; results go to /tmp/attnbench/<run-id>.json
- Postprocess: tools/attn_bench/agg.py --input /tmp/attnbench/<run-id>.json --output /tmp/attnbench/agg-<run-id>.json

Contact and ownership:
- Primary owner: Aisha Patel (eng-serving-runtime) — responsible for coordinating the initial selector merge and runbook updates.
- SME for paged-attn: Marco Ruiz.
- SME for fused-op kernels: Daniel Kim.

Last notes (informal):
- This doc is deliberately pragmatic: start with the cheap heuristics above, measure widely, and only introduce more complex ML-based routing if simple rules don't meet SLOs.
- Keep microbench harness small and reproducible; avoid full Nsight in routine runs — reserve for deep dives.

Change log:
